predictions.explanation:
Evidence indicates this prediction came true.

- Around the time of the podcast, the *average* U.S. used-car price had indeed “spiked to about $29,000”: Edmunds data reported by AP put the average used-vehicle price at roughly $29,011 in late 2021, widely cited as “about $29,000,” and Cox data show average listing prices hovering a bit above $28,000 into spring 2022. ([kvia.com](https://kvia.com/news/business-technology/ap-national-business/2022/01/03/29000-for-an-average-used-car-would-be-buyers-are-aghast/?utm_source=openai))
- One year later, in May 2023, Cox Automotive/Kelley Blue Book report that the average used-vehicle listing/transaction price was $27,256, i.e., clearly *below* $29,000. ([kbb.com](https://www.kbb.com/car-news/average-used-car-price-topped-27000-in-may/?utm_source=openai))
- Over that same March 2022–May 2023 period, the Federal Reserve raised the federal funds rate from near 0% to a 5.0–5.25% target range, and data show average used-car loan APRs rising from about 14.1% in May 2022 to about 16.0% in May 2023, making financing more expensive. ([bankrate.com](https://www.bankrate.com/banking/federal-reserve/history-of-federal-funds-rate/?utm_source=openai))  Cox Automotive explicitly noted in late 2022 that higher interest rates were beginning to hurt used-vehicle demand and could push dealers to lower prices. ([coxautoinc.com](https://www.coxautoinc.com/insights-hub/used-vehicle-inventory-september-2022/?utm_source=openai))

Because the average used-car price by roughly May 2023 was noticeably *lower* than the cited ~$29,000 level, the core quantitative claim of the prediction was correct; the suggested mechanism (demand destruction from higher interest rates) is also consistent with contemporaneous commentary, though multiple factors influenced prices.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence from the U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) shows that inflation did in fact “roll over” from its early‑2022 pace over the months following May 2022, although there were a couple of additional hot prints before the clear downshift.

1. **Context at the time of the prediction (May 23, 2022)**  
   - The latest data then available were for April 2022: headline CPI rose **0.3% month‑over‑month** after a very hot **1.2% in March**, suggesting a tentative cooling in sequential inflation. ([bls.gov](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/cpi_05112022.htm?utm_source=openai))

2. **Immediate subsequent prints (May–June 2022)**  
   - The May 2022 CPI release later showed a **1.0% m/m** gain for “all items,” re‑accelerating from April’s 0.3%. ([bls.gov](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/cpi_06102022.htm?utm_source=openai))  
   - The June 2022 release showed an even hotter **1.3% m/m** with a **9.1% y/y** inflation rate, the peak of the cycle. ([bls.gov](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/cpi_07132022.htm?mf_ct_campaign=yahoo-synd-feed&utm_source=openai))  
   - So in the *very* short run (May–June), inflation did not yet roll over; it briefly intensified.

3. **Behavior in the “ensuing months” after the mid‑2022 peak**  
   - A BLS‑derived summary table of monthly changes shows:  
     - **All items CPI m/m:** May 2022 = 1.0%, June = 1.3%, then **July = 0.0%, August = 0.1%, September = 0.4%, October = 0.4%, November = 0.1%.** ([usinflation.org](https://usinflation.org/us-inflation-release-dates/?utm_source=openai))  
   - These post‑June prints are dramatically lower than the 0.6%–1.3% range seen in early 2022, indicating a clear rollover in the *sequential* pace of inflation even though the level of prices remained high.

4. **Peak and subsequent trend in year‑over‑year inflation**  
   - BLS data on 12‑month changes show headline CPI **peaking at 9.1% in June 2022**, then falling to **8.5% (July), 8.3% (August), 8.2% (September), 7.7% (October), 7.1% (November), 6.5% (December)**, and continuing to decline to about **3.0% by June 2023**. ([bls.gov](https://www.bls.gov/beta/nextgen/cpi/consumer-price-index-2023-10-12.htm?utm_source=openai))  
   - Later summaries note that inflation **peaked at 9.1% in June 2022** and then, after staying ≥6% for about 17 months, fell below **3% by late 2024**. ([usinflationcalculator.com](https://www.usinflationcalculator.com/inflation/u-s-inflation-rises-0-3-in-june-annual-rate-hits-2-7/100059114/?utm_source=openai))  
   - By mid‑2025, annual CPI is in the **mid‑2% range**, far below the 8–9% zone of spring–summer 2022. ([usinflationcalculator.com](https://www.usinflationcalculator.com/inflation/u-s-inflation-rises-0-3-in-june-annual-rate-hits-2-7/100059114/?utm_source=openai))

5. **Assessment versus the normalized prediction**  
   - The normalized claim is that U.S. inflation would **decline from peak levels on a sequential month‑over‑month basis over the ensuing months**, rather than remain at or above its then‑current elevated pace.
   - The data show:
     - A final lurch higher in May–June 2022, with CPI m/m at 1.0–1.3%. ([bls.gov](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/cpi_06102022.htm?utm_source=openai))  
     - Starting in **July 2022**, monthly increases fell to 0.0–0.4% and stayed far below the earlier 1%+ readings, which is exactly the sort of rollover in sequential inflation he was describing. ([usinflation.org](https://usinflation.org/us-inflation-release-dates/?utm_source=openai))  
     - Over the following year and beyond, year‑over‑year inflation decisively trended down from the June 2022 peak rather than persisting around 8–9%. ([bls.gov](https://www.bls.gov/beta/nextgen/cpi/consumer-price-index-2023-10-12.htm?utm_source=openai))

Given that inflation soon peaked and, from mid‑2022 onward, the *month‑to‑month* pace of price increases and the *year‑over‑year* rate both moved lower instead of staying near their prior extremes, the prediction that inflation would "roll" rather than remain stuck at its elevated pace is **substantively correct**, even though it was a bit early relative to the final June spike.

predictions.grok_explanation: US CPI-U seasonally adjusted month-over-month (MoM) inflation peaked at 1.0% in both May and June 2022 (BLS releases: [May 2022](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/cpi_06102022.pdf), [June 2022](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/cpi_07132022.pdf)). In ensuing months after May 2022, it declined sharply rather than remaining at elevated ~1% pace: July 2022: 0.0%, August: +0.1%, September: +0.4%, October: +0.4%, November: +0.1%, December: -0.1% (BLS archives and [YCharts data](https://ycharts.com/indicators/us_consumer_price_index_mom)). It continued fluctuating but stayed low (mostly 0.0-0.5%) through 2023-2025, averaging ~0.2-0.3%, confirming rollover (FRED CPIAUCSL trends, BLS CPI summaries). This matches the prediction of MoM decline from peaks over ensuing months, not sustained high pace.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence since May 2022 supports E’s view that the U.S. would not enter a persistent “hyper‑inflation” regime and that longer‑term inflation expectations would point to moderating, not runaway, inflation.

* **Realized inflation moderated rather than exploded.** BLS data show annual CPI inflation of about **8.0% in 2022**, falling to **4.1% in 2023** and **about 3.0% in 2024**.([bls.gov](https://www.bls.gov/pir/spm/spm_chart6_2024data.htm?utm_source=openai)) By early 2025, year‑over‑year CPI was around **2.8%**, down sharply from the 2022 peak above 9%.([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2025/mar/12/februrary-inflation-rate?utm_source=openai)) This is elevated but clearly a *cooling* pattern, not continuously accelerating prices.
* **10‑year TIPS breakeven inflation has stayed in a normal, anchored range.** FRED’s 10‑year breakeven series shows the market’s expected 10‑year inflation was **2.69% in May 2022**, then moved down into roughly the **2.1–2.4%** band through 2023–2025; recent daily values are around **2.2–2.3%**.([fred.stlouisfed.org](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/T10YIEM)) This is consistent with moderate, near‑target inflation expectations rather than an expectation of sustained very high or explosive inflation.
* **No sign of actual hyperinflation.** In standard economics (Cagan), *hyperinflation* is defined as monthly inflation above **50%**, which the U.S. never came close to; even at the 2022 peak, monthly CPI changes were in the low single digits.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperinflation?utm_source=openai))

Given that (1) actual inflation has clearly rolled over from its 2022 highs toward the low‑single‑digit range and (2) 10‑year breakeven rates have remained around ~2–2.5% instead of blowing out, the bond market has indeed been signaling moderating, not runaway, inflation. That aligns with E’s claim that investors should not believe the “hyper inflation narrative.”

predictions.explanation:
By late 2025, it’s still too early to definitively judge either vintage window E described.

**1. Evidence on the “last 18 months” (roughly late 2020–May 2022)**

* Funds whose main deployment coincided with the 2021–early‑2022 peak do look weak so far:
  * Carta’s fund‑performance data show that the 2021 and 2022 VC vintages have **negative median IRRs and median TVPI below 1×**, and they underperform the 2017–2020 vintages when compared at the same number of quarters since inception. ([landonhowell.com](https://www.landonhowell.com/notes/new-startup-fundraising-landscape?utm_source=openai))  
  * Institutional Investor, citing PitchBook, notes that **2021 vintage VC funds have a negative pooled IRR**, with analysts expecting further declines, and also highlights elevated rates of flat/down rounds in 2024–2025. ([institutionalinvestor.com](https://www.institutionalinvestor.com/article/venture-capitals-woes-could-get-worse?utm_source=openai))  
  * Carta and related analyses point out much lower graduation rates from seed to Series A and from Series A to B for companies funded in 2021–2022 than for cohorts a few years earlier, consistent with weaker portfolio quality and returns pressure. ([landonhowell.com](https://www.landonhowell.com/notes/new-startup-fundraising-landscape?utm_source=openai))  

These early signals are directionally consistent with E’s claim that the “vintage of the last 18 months will be lousy.” But they are **far from final**:

* Venture funds typically take 7–10+ years to realize their true returns, and even 2017–2018 vintages still haven’t fully distributed capital. ([carta.com](https://carta.com/uk/en/data/vc-fund-performance-q4-2024/?utm_source=openai))  
* Commentary on the same Carta data explicitly warns that IRR/TVPI and quartile rankings for vintages 2021–2022 are not very reliable until about year 5–6. ([magmapartners.com](https://magmapartners.com/post/magma-partners-q2-2024-investor-letter?utm_source=openai))  

So while early performance of the 2021–2022 deployment period looks poor, we **cannot yet say with confidence** that those vintages will ultimately be “lousy” on a final realized‑return basis.

**2. Evidence on the “upcoming vintage” (2022–2023 onward)**

E also predicted that the vintage immediately following May 2022 would be “a good vintage.” Here the data are even less conclusive:

* Carta’s Q1 2024 and subsequent updates show that **2022 vintage median IRR remains negative and median TVPI is still below 1×**, lagging earlier vintages at the same age. ([landonhowell.com](https://www.landonhowell.com/notes/new-startup-fundraising-landscape?utm_source=openai))  
* Early reports for the 2023 vintage show **very strong top‑decile IRRs (>30%) driven by AI‑related markups**, but the **median performance for 2023 funds isn’t yet clearly strong** and DPI is only just beginning to appear. ([sourcery.vc](https://www.sourcery.vc/p/breaking-cartas-vc-fund-performance?utm_source=openai))  

Given that these funds are only ~2–3 years into their lives, their ultimate performance could still swing significantly as exits (or write‑downs) materialize.

**3. Overall assessment**

* Early data broadly **support the intuition** that capital deployed at the very top of the 2021–early‑2022 bubble is struggling, relative to prior “cheaper” vintages.  
* However, both the allegedly “lousy” vintage (late‑2020–2022) and the supposedly “good” follow‑on vintage (2022–2023+) are **too young** to judge by normal venture standards, and respected analyses of the same datasets caution against drawing firm conclusions this early. ([magmapartners.com](https://magmapartners.com/post/magma-partners-q2-2024-investor-letter?utm_source=openai))  

Because these outcomes won’t be knowable with high confidence until closer to the early‑2030s, the correct classification as of November 2025 is **“inconclusive (too early)”**, even though preliminary evidence leans in the direction E anticipated for the 2021–2022 period.

predictions.explanation:
The prediction said that the peak asset prices of late‑2020–early‑2022, especially in venture and high‑growth equities, would *not* be seen again under normal conditions and would require something like another pandemic or nuclear war that forces interest rates back to zero.

What actually happened by late 2025:

- **Broad high‑growth equity indices exceeded their 2021 peaks under higher‑than‑zero rates and without a new pandemic or nuclear war.** The Nasdaq Composite, which hit a then‑record in November 2021, went on to set new all‑time highs in February 2024 and again in June 2025, reaching over 20,000—well above its 2021 peak. ([investinglive.com](https://investinglive.com/news/nasdaq-index-closes-at-an-all-time-record-high-highest-close-since-november-2021-20240229/?utm_source=openai))
- **Monetary policy never returned to zero rates during this run‑up.** The federal funds rate was 0% through late 2021, but then was hiked to a peak 5.25–5.50% in 2023, and as of October 2025 is still 3.75–4.00%—well above zero—while equities trade near record levels. ([ycharts.com](https://ycharts.com/indicators/target_federal_funds_rate?utm_source=openai)) This directly contradicts the claim that those prices would only come back if rates went back to zero.
- **Top private “venture / cloud / AI” valuations are at new record highs.** Bessemer’s 2025 Cloud 100 report shows the aggregate valuation of the top 100 private cloud companies at $1.117 trillion, a record and up 36% from 2024, even though average revenue multiples have fallen ~41% from their 2021 peak. ([bvp.com](https://www.bvp.com/atlas/the-cloud-100-benchmarks-report/?utm_source=openai)) Within that group, AI leaders such as OpenAI (~$500B), Anthropic (~$183B), and Databricks (> $100B) have private valuations that substantially exceed almost any 2021 venture valuation, achieved without a return to zero rates. ([bvp.com](https://www.bvp.com/atlas/the-cloud-100-benchmarks-report/?utm_source=openai))
- **Public proxies for emerging cloud/high‑growth also show prices revisiting or approaching bubble levels.** The WisdomTree Cloud Computing Fund (WCLD), which tracks the BVP Nasdaq Emerging Cloud Index, reached an all‑time high of $41.87 on December 9, 2024, surpassing prior peaks, with Fed funds still over 4%. ([stockscan.io](https://stockscan.io/stocks/WCLD/price-history?utm_source=openai)) The underlying BVP Emerging Cloud Index (EMCLOUD) has been trading around 1,600–1,700 in 2025, far above its 2018 base and reflecting a strong recovery in public cloud valuations. ([indexes.nasdaqomx.com](https://indexes.nasdaqomx.com/index/overview/emcloud?utm_source=openai))

There *are* parts of the market where his caution was directionally right:

- Many of the specific 2020–2021 darlings remain far below their peaks. ARK Innovation ETF’s price is still roughly half its February 2021 all‑time high (~$160 vs. ~mid‑70s–80s in late 2025). ([stockscan.io](https://stockscan.io/stocks/ARKK/price-history?utm_source=openai)) Individual high‑beta cloud names like 8x8 and nCino have valuations 65–95% below their all‑time highs. ([trueup.io](https://www.trueup.io/co/8x8?utm_source=openai)) And venture revenue multiples overall are materially below 2021 levels. ([bvp.com](https://www.bvp.com/atlas/the-cloud-100-benchmarks-report/?utm_source=openai))

However, the prediction was framed broadly—“prices we saw in the world over the last 18 months…we’re not getting back there…unless…rates go to zero.” In reality, by 2024–2025 many major equity indices and leading venture/AI names *did* surpass their 2021 nominal price levels under normal (non‑zero) rate conditions and without the extreme shocks he specified. That makes the prediction, taken as stated, **wrong**, even though it captured the persistent reset in *multiples* and in many of the bubbliest names.

predictions.explanation:
The prediction was that, over the three years after May 2022, only about **$25–30B** of the roughly **$100B** of “real” VC capital within a supposed **$250B** “quarter‑trillion” pool would actually be deployed into venture deals (≈$8–10B per year of *total* VC dollars), with most of the overall $250B instead deployed by traditional PE/LBO firms. In other words, it implied an extremely small annual flow of VC capital into startups.

What actually happened:

* **Global VC deal activity** remained vastly larger than the predicted ~$8–10B/year:
  * 2022 global VC funding totaled **$435.7B**, per S&P Global Market Intelligence; 2023 totaled **$260B**.([spglobal.com](https://www.spglobal.com/market-intelligence/en/news-insights/articles/2024/1/global-venture-capital-investments-continue-downtrend-in-december-2023-80043834?utm_source=openai))  
  * 2024 global VC investment came in on the order of **$314–368B** depending on the source (Crunchbase via Barron’s vs KPMG’s Venture Pulse).([barrons.com](https://www.barrons.com/articles/venture-capital-investments-2024-ai-766c99dc?utm_source=openai))  
  Even if you only count the period **after** the podcast (roughly H2 2022–end 2024), that’s **hundreds of billions of dollars** in VC investments, orders of magnitude above $25–30B.

* **U.S. VC alone** massively exceeds the forecast “$8B per year” notion:
  * NVCA/PitchBook data show **$170.6B** of U.S. VC deals in 2023.([nvca.org](https://nvca.org/press_releases/nvca-2024-yearbook-charting-the-new-path-forward-for-venture-capital/?utm_source=openai))  
  * PitchBook data reported by Reuters show **$209B** of U.S. VC funding in 2024.([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/ai-startups-drive-vc-funding-resurgence-capturing-record-us-investment-2024-2025-01-07/?utm_source=openai))  
  That’s nearly **$380B** over just 2023–24 in one country, versus the podcast’s implied global run rate of ~$24–30B over three years.

* **Dry powder data** also contradict the idea that only a tiny fraction of committed VC capital would ever be deployed:
  * Axios, using PitchBook, reported **$298.5B** of U.S. VC dry powder as of Sept. 30, 2022.([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2023/01/14/venture-capital-dry-powder-2023?utm_source=openai))  
  * NVCA’s 2024 Yearbook shows U.S. VC firms ending 2023 with **$311.6B** in dry powder and **$1.21T** under management.([nvca.org](https://nvca.org/press_releases/nvca-2024-yearbook-charting-the-new-path-forward-for-venture-capital/?utm_source=openai))  
  * Other analyses in 2024–25 similarly place global VC dry powder around **$300B+**, not near-zero, and not a world in which only ~$25–30B ever got deployed from the 2021–22 vintages.([eisneramper.com](https://www.eisneramper.com/insights/financial-services/venture-capital-q1-vc-blog-2024/?utm_source=openai))  
  These figures imply large, ongoing deployment of VC funds (alongside continued fundraising), not a scenario where just ~25–30% of a $100B VC slice is used over three years.

* On the **PE vs VC mix**, broad industry data do show that **buyout/private‑equity deal value remains much larger than classic VC**, and PE/LBO firms continued to deploy trillions globally. McKinsey’s 2025 Global Private Markets report, for example, estimates **$2T** in global private equity and venture investments in 2024, with roughly **$1.5T** from buyout firms alone and dry powder still above **$2T**.([bebeez.eu](https://bebeez.eu/2025/02/14/in-2024-global-investments-of-private-equity-and-venture-funds-amounted-to-2-trillion-us-dollars-14-dry-powder-is-worth-2-1-trillion-11-yoy-mckinsey-says/?utm_source=openai))  That makes the *directional* claim (“buyout firms will deploy the bulk of the capital”) broadly reasonable — but it doesn’t rescue the very specific **$25–30B** limit he attached to VC deployment.

Given:

* the speaker explicitly characterized this as **“like eight billion of total VC dollars deployed a year”**, and
* observed VC deal volumes (both globally and in the U.S.) are **one to two orders of magnitude larger** than that over the relevant three‑year window,

the quantitative core of the prediction — that only ~$25–30B of VC dollars would be deployed over those three years — is decisively contradicted by realized investment data.

Therefore, the prediction is **wrong** overall, even though the qualitative intuition that PE/LBO activity would dominate in aggregate was directionally consistent with later market statistics.

predictions.grok_explanation:
The prediction claimed only ~$25-30B of VC capital (25-30% of ~$100B VC portion in $250B committed funds) would be deployed into venture deals from May 2022-May 2025, with most of the $250B by PE/LBO firms. This did not occur.

US VC invested far more: 2022 total $236B ([NVCA Q3 2025 Venture Monitor](https://nvca.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Q3-2025-PitchBook-NVCA-Venture-Monitor.pdf)); 2023 $166B; 2024 $216B; H1 2025 $163B ([NVCA Q2 2025](https://nvca.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Q2-2025-PitchBook-NVCA-Venture-Monitor-19728.pdf)). Period sum (approx. H2 2022 + 2023 + 2024 + H1 2025) >$650B, including ~$25B May 2022 onward adjustment.

VC dry powder (context for $250-290B in 2022, e.g., [PitchBook Oct 2022](https://pitchbook.com/news/articles/dry-powder-save-startups-vc)) reached record $311B by 2025 ([NVCA Q3 2025](https://nvca.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Q3-2025-PitchBook-NVCA-Venture-Monitor.pdf)), piling up due to fundraising despite high deployment. 2022-vintage funds deployed 67% capital by Q2 2025 (~3 years; [Carta Q2 2025](https://carta.com/data/vc-fund-performance-q2-2025/)), vs. predicted 25-30%.

VC deployment vastly exceeded $25-30B; slowdown happened but not to predicted extent.

predictions.explanation: Market data from 2021–2025 strongly supports the *direction* of the prediction but cannot yet conclusively settle its strongest claims. Across public and private SaaS, revenue multiples have compressed dramatically from the 2021 bubble: median public SaaS EV/revenue fell from roughly 18–20x at the peak to about 6–8x by 2024–2025, with private deals commonly in the 4–6x range, i.e., back near pre‑boom norms and 60–70% below the highs. ([windsordrake.com](https://windsordrake.com/saas-valuation-multiples/?utm_source=openai)) Contemporary analyses document that in 2021–early 2022 many late‑stage SaaS companies in roughly the $50–80M ARR band raised at 50–100x ARR, and now face a world where public comps trade closer to 6–8x; even assuming ~60% annual growth and a return to ~10x public multiples, such companies need years merely to grow into their last-round valuations, implying substantial risk of down rounds and weak returns for investors who bought at the top. ([medium.com](https://medium.com/stellaris-venture-partners/why-saas-companies-can-withstand-the-funding-downcycle-better-a8369f681aa8?utm_source=openai)) That evidence is very consistent with the speaker’s core view that the 100x‑ARR pricing for typical software names in 2020–2021 was a bubble and that investors in those rounds are, as of 2025, deeply underwater on paper. However, the prediction went further, asserting that such companies are highly likely *never* to see those price levels again and that investor returns from those rounds will be *absolutely* eviscerated. Many of the affected companies remain private or only a few years past those financings, and venture outcomes normally play out over a decade or more; some high-profile software/AI names are again securing 50–100x+ ARR multiples in 2023–2025 (for example, Wiz and several frontier AI startups like Perplexity AI), showing that extreme revenue multiples can reappear for certain categories and narratives. ([fabricaventures.com](https://fabricaventures.com/100x-arr/?utm_source=openai)) It is also plausible that a subset of the 2020–2021 100x‑ARR cohort ultimately grows revenue enough over many years to deliver acceptable or even strong investor returns, despite today’s compressed multiples. Because (a) the long‑run outcomes for that cohort are not yet observable, (b) the time horizon implied by words like ‘never’ and ‘absolutely eviscerated’ extends well beyond 2025, and (c) we already see counterexamples where very high multiples have resurfaced in adjacent parts of software, the strongest form of the prediction cannot yet be definitively classified as right or wrong. On the evidence available in late 2025, it remains unresolved rather than proven, so the fairest assessment is that the prediction is still inconclusive (too early).

Commentary confirms 2021 high-multiple companies face permanent resets due to dilution and growth deceleration ([Elad Gil](https://blog.eladgil.com/p/startup-decoupling-and-reckoning), [Clouded Judgement](https://cloudedjudgement.substack.com/p/clouded-judgement-11224-hard-truths)); no examples of such firms regaining 100x levels by 2025.

predictions.explanation:
By mid‑2022, U.S. headline CPI inflation peaked around 9% year‑over‑year during the pandemic surge, but then fell markedly: BLS-based averages drop from about 8.0% in 2022 to 4.1% in 2023, 2.9% in 2024, and roughly 2.3–2.7% so far in 2025, with 12‑month CPI running near 3%. This is a clear rollover of the 2020–22 spike rather than a shift to permanently very high inflation. ([usinflationcalculator.com](https://www.usinflationcalculator.com/inflation/annual-averages-for-rate-of-inflation/?utm_source=openai))

Before COVID (roughly 2000–2019), U.S. inflation mostly ran in a low band of about 1.5–2.5% per year. ([usinflationcalculator.com](https://www.usinflationcalculator.com/inflation/annual-averages-for-rate-of-inflation/?utm_source=openai)) Today’s realized inflation of about 2.5–3% is only modestly above that range, and medium‑term forecasts for CPI over the next five years cluster around ~2.4–2.5%, which is close to the pre‑pandemic norm and well below the peak of the spike. ([ycharts.com](https://ycharts.com/indicators/median_forecasts_for_cpi_inflation_over_5_years?utm_source=openai))

Some central‑bank and academic work does argue that structural forces—like deglobalization, tighter labor markets, and higher green or defense spending—may keep inflation somewhat higher or more persistent than in the 2000–2019 era, and the Federal Reserve’s own projections now see inflation above its 2% target for several more years. ([frbsf.org](https://www.frbsf.org/research-and-insights/publications/economic-letter/2023/03/forward-looking-policy-in-real-time-world?utm_source=openai)) But even these analyses envisage inflation converging to low single digits rather than remaining at the 2021–22 highs.

Given that (1) the 2020–22 inflation spike has decisively rolled over and (2) inflation has returned to a low, near‑pre‑COVID range rather than a new high‑inflation regime, E’s qualitative prediction—that we would look back and see the spike as transitory, with something like the earlier disinflationary environment reasserting itself—has been borne out by the data available through late 2025.

predictions.grok_explanation: US CPI inflation spiked to a peak of 9.1% in June 2022 (annual 6.5%), confirming the 2020-2022 spike. It subsequently rolled over, declining to 3.4% in 2023, 2.9% in 2024, and 3.0% YoY as of September 2025 ([US Inflation Calculator](https://www.usinflationcalculator.com/inflation/current-inflation-rates/), BLS CPI releases). Pre-COVID (2000-2019), annual CPI averaged ~2.1% with rates mostly 1-3%, a disinflationary trend of low/stable inflation. Post-peak, inflation has returned to this ~2-3% range, with disinflation continuing (though slowing), as noted in CEPR's 'rise and retreat' analysis and Fed reports (PCE at 2.6-2.9% in late 2024/2025). Looking back from 2025, the spike appears temporary, and low-inflation trends have resumed ([Trading Economics](https://tradingeconomics.com/united-states/inflation-cpi), [FRED CPIAUCSL](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CPIAUCSL)).

predictions.explanation:
Using broad large‑cap growth proxies, the core, time‑bound part of the prediction—that “growth stocks” would be *higher* roughly one year later, after potentially going lower in the interim—did come true, though the more specific claim about valuations reverting to trend is not well supported by the data.

**1. Were growth stocks higher by around May 2023 than in May 2022?**

- The Invesco QQQ ETF (a common proxy for large‑cap U.S. growth via the Nasdaq‑100) traded in a roughly $301–308 range in May 2022 and a roughly $343–348 range in May 2023, meaning May 2023 levels were clearly higher than a year earlier.
  ([digrin.com](https://www.digrin.com/stocks/detail/QQQ/price?utm_source=openai))
- Index ETFs tracking the Russell 1000 Growth Index, such as IWF and VONG, had very strong returns in calendar 2023 (about +42–43%) after a deep drawdown in 2022 (about –29%), implying that by mid‑/late‑2023 they were well above their 2022 levels.
  ([financecharts.com](https://www.financecharts.com/etfs/IWF/performance?utm_source=openai))
- FTSE Russell’s 2023 style commentary notes that growth and technology “retook the lead” over value over the year ending April 28, 2023, consistent with a rebound in large‑cap growth stocks over the period the prediction covered.
  ([lseg.com](https://www.lseg.com/en/media-centre/press-releases/ftse-russell/2023/ftse-russell-begins-35th-annual-russell-us-indexes-reconstitution?utm_source=openai))

**2. Did we “get there by way of lower and potentially meaningfully lower” prices?**

- QQQ fell about 33% in 2022, substantially underperforming the S&P 500’s roughly 19% decline, reflecting a sharp drawdown in large‑cap growth/tech during the tightening cycle before recovering in 2023.
  ([marketwatch.com](https://www.marketwatch.com/story/tech-stocks-seem-to-have-ended-their-difficult-relationship-with-the-bond-market-88d90759?utm_source=openai))
- The Russell 1000 Growth proxy ETFs (IWF, VONG) show large negative total returns in 2022 (around –29%), followed by a powerful rebound in 2023, matching the “down first, then up” path described in the quote.
  ([financecharts.com](https://www.financecharts.com/etfs/IWF/performance?utm_source=openai))

**3. Did valuations revert toward their recent historical averages?**

- A Q1 2023 letter from Boyar Value Group reports that large‑cap growth (Russell 1000 Growth) was trading at about 23.8× earnings versus a long‑term average around 20.8×—still meaningfully above its historical norm rather than “back to” it.
  ([gurufocus.com](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/1974483/boyar-value-groups-1stquarter-2023-letter?utm_source=openai))
- Later analyses reinforce that elevated growth valuations persisted: a 2024 BlackRock note cites the Russell 1000 Growth at 32.8× earnings versus a 15‑year average of 25.0×, and BofA/Glenmede work referenced by MarketWatch places large‑cap growth valuations in the 90‑plus percentile versus history.
  ([blackrock.com](https://www.blackrock.com/us/financial-professionals/insights/why-now-for-active-value?utm_source=openai))

**Assessment**

- **Correct:**
  - Growth‑stock benchmarks (QQQ, Russell 1000 Growth) were significantly higher by roughly May 2023 than in May 2022.
  - The path involved a large intervening drawdown in 2022 before the rebound, as anticipated.
- **Partially/Not supported:**
  - Valuations did *not* clearly “bounce back” merely to five‑year (or long‑term) averages; evidence shows they remained above historical norms.

Given that the clearly falsifiable core of the prediction (direction and timing of growth‑stock prices, with an intervening selloff) was borne out, while the valuation‑normalization detail was off, the overall judgment is **“right”** rather than ambiguous.
